articles.text: The Piedmont School Board announced on June 14 that Ariel Dolowich will take over as the district’s new Curriculum Director and Assistant Superintendent as of July 1. He most recently was with Newark Unified School District as its Director of Teaching and Learning for the past four years. The job included leading professional development for principals and staff, providing district-wide communication for certificated and classified staff, designing and presenting Town Hall meetings, and partnering with during labor negotiations. “The Assistant Superintendent position will be a promotion for him, with increased responsibility that includes the duties that are typical in a curriculum director position,” explained incoming Piedmont Superintendent Jennifer Hawn. “Dr. Hawn was participating in the [hiring] process, which I think is very appropriate. [Hawn and Dolowich] will be working so closely together and [they] look like a good team already,” said board member Cory Smegal. The school board has agreed to a three-year contract at $180,000 per year. Dolowich replaces Cheryl Wozniak. Dolowich is an active leadership coach of principals with Alameda County Office of Education. His resume also includes nine years as the Principal of Ochoa Middle School in Hayward. “I was really impressed by the breadth of Ariel’s experience and the recognition that he has received from his peers in education and just his thoughtfulness in responding to our questions,” said School Board President Veronica Anderson-Thigpen. Ariel Dolowich, Piedmont School District’s new Curriculum Director, lives in the East Bay with his wife and three children.

articles.text: Editor: In a letter published on May 24, I expressed the opinion that the City should not (as proposed in the U.C. Berkeley graduate students’ development concept) hand over land with a value of $7 million for 103 affordable-housing apartments, given that we soon will need to spend tens of millions of dollars to upgrade the City’s civic center. (In contrast, land for 30 market-rate townhomes would be purchased from the City for $5.3 million.) A letter by Jerry Kennelly published on May 31 explained why the apartment development concept is not financially realistic under any circumstances, thus giving me hope that this particular land grab will not take place. However, Piedmonters should be aware that City staff (and, apparently, the City Council) have been ready to give away City land for quite some time. Quoting portions of answers to Frequently Asked Questions set forth at https://www.piedmontishome.org/faqs: • “The City could choose to sell land at fair market value, or could sell or lease its land for low cost to an affordable housing developer in exchange for the provision of affordable housing.” • “[D]ue to the high cost of land in Piedmont, it is generally understood that a multi-family affordable housing development in Piedmont will only be economically feasible if the land is provided at little or no cost.” • “The City is not obligated to enter into any agreement and is able to pursue a process in its own best interest.” I urge Piedmonters to let the City Council and City staff know that giving away City land, whether for a period of years or in perpetuity, is not in our best interest: • Providing land at little or no cost may help a few hundred new residents, but it will constitute an inappropriate taking of property, or proceeds thereof, from more than 10,000 existing residents. • Nothing in the Housing Element or applicable State law requires such a taking. • Those who are eager to see affordable-housing apartments built should look for a way to pay for the land, such as via philanthropic organizations. –Dana H. Despite various safe storage laws regarding children, 4.6 million kids live in a home with an unlocked, loaded gun. articles.text: As summer arrives, Piedmont adults and youth have a wealth of opportunities to explore local volunteer work. There are several volunteer opportunities this summer at the Oakland Zoo for those who love working with animals. You can work alongside a zookeeper assisting with daily animal care, as a conservation volunteer interpreting the Zoo’s conservation initiatives to guests, or as a docent sharing your passion for wildlife and conservation with Zoo visitors. There are also a variety of internships available to teens and adults in seasonal (fall, winter, and summer) sessions. To learn more about volunteer programs at the Zoo, visit oaklandzoo.org/ volunteer-and-internship-opportunities. Piedmont Center for the Arts Throughout the year, the all-volunteer-run, nonprofit Piedmont Center for the Arts hosts theater shows, visual arts exhibits, music performances, literary events, and more. Volunteers do everything — from production, carpentry, and painting to hosting receptions for events, handling box office duties, set design, and costuming. The PCA particularly needs volunteers to staff the galleries and to assist at other events. To learn more and get involved, email the PCA at info@piedmontcenterforthearts.org. Museum of Children’s Art (MOCHA) Students who have a love of art and are interested in the education field would enjoy volunteering at the Museum of Children’s Art (MOCHA) in Oakland this summer. Tasks include everything from preparing art materials, to aiding youth art workshops and afterschool library events, to assisting with special events at the museum. Email info@mocha. org for volunteer inquiries. Visit mocha.org to learn more about summer events at the museum. Alameda County Community Food Bank The Alameda County Community Food Bank needs volunteers to prepare food in the ACCFB Oakland warehouse, and to help distribute food at neighborhood distribution sites throughout the county. For a full list of volunteer needs at local pantries and other organizations, email volunteer@ accfd.org, or visit accfb.org/get-involved/volunteer. A calendar of all volunteer opportunities for adults and youth 10 years old and up is available at accfb.org/get-involved/volunteer-calendar. Donations are also welcome. articles.text: Block party street closure applications due June 28 This year’s 4th of July Parade, with a theme of “Paint the Town Red, White, and Blue,” will begin on Tuesday, July 4, at 11 a.m. on Highland Avenue. One of Piedmont’s oldest and most beloved traditions, the parade, now in its 56th year, features floats from neighborhoods and community organizations, a rich array of antique and classic cars, and several bagpipe bands in keeping with Piedmont’s Scottish traditions. Pancake breakfast An all-you-can eat pancake breakfast will take place before the parade from 8 to 10 a.m. at the Veterans Hall. The breakfast is operated each year by the Piedmont Community Service Crew, a coed venturing unit with the Piedmont Scouts. Sausages are provided by Piedmont Grocery and fresh fruit is provided by Village Market. Tickets for the breakfast are $15 for age 15 and up, $10 for youth age three to 14, and free for children under three. Tickets are available at the door or may be purchased in advance online at bit.ly/3CDO3Zu. Applications are due by 5 p.m. on Wednesday, June 28. The city will confirm approval of applicants by Friday, June 30, and the Public Works Department will deliver barricades to streets on Monday, July 3. articles.text: David Hopkins, a longtime Supervisor of the before-school and after-school Schoolmates program, will be Grand Marshal of this year’s 4th of July parade, the 56th annual. Hopkins will be retiring after this summer and 34 years with the Recreation Department. “I love this community,” he said. “This is above and beyond – that people want me to be part of this. I’ve always been in the parade. It’s such a huge honor. I can’t begin to tell you.” This year the Parade Committee has a new chair for the first time in over two decades. Kathy Kelleher, the daughter of parade founder Dick Johnson, and a member of the committee for many years, will take over the duties of Carla Betts who served as chair for 20 years. On selecting Hopkins, Kelleher said, “It was an easy decision. He’s the right guy. He is retiring and we appreciate all that he’s done for our community,” said Kelleher. “He sort of transcends through generations. He has made me smile, he made my kids smile, and he is a good guy.” Asked to describe the duties of a Grand Marshal, Kelleher said, “It’s about honoring them all day. They ride in the parade, and they get to judge the parade entries and decide the awards. Then there’s an area blocked off for them in the park for the music afterwards.” Hopkins is known for wearing a tank top regardless of the weather. articles.text: Bagpipes in Piedmont have been a tradition since 1932 when football coach Glen “Brick” Johnson started the Kiltie Band at Piedmont High School. Today, the Piedmont Highlanders Drums and Pipes is a community band performing in parades and at special events throughout the Bay Area. Band members wear a traditional Scottish military style uniform of the Seaforth Highlanders which wore MacKenzie tartan kilts. The band officers include Pipe Major Ellison Dunlap, Jr.; Drum Sergeant Nancy Dunlap amd Band Manager Fred Rutledge. The band regularly performs at the Scottish Highland Games at the Dunsmuir Estate in Oakland, on John Muir Day at the Muir Estate in Martinez, and in the St. Patrick Day Parade in Dublin. It has performed at the Tartan Day Games at Ardenwood Historic Farm in Fremont and in the Celtic Festival in Fremont. It is the opening band at the Alameda County Fair Parade in Pleasanton. The Piedmont Highlanders have played at Grace Cathedral on Armistice Day and at the San Francisco Giants ballpark at the opening game of the baseball playoffs. The band has won ribbons as best band in the Newark parade, at the Walnut Festival in Walnut Creek, and in the Annual Piedmont 4th of July Parade. For additional information, contact Ellison Dunlap at 465- 3699. Photo of Highlander bagpipe band

articles.text: An excited, energetic group of 40 recent eighth grade graduates from Piedmont Middle School met before dawn on June 3 to embark on a tour of Washington, D.C. with organizers and parent chaperones Stacy Morgan, Kim Hunter, and Sabrina Smith. They spent five jam-packed days touring sites in the nation’s capital including the Lincoln Memorial, Jefferson Memorial, Arlington Cemetery, the National Archives, the Holocaust Museum, the Martin Luther King, Jr. Memorial, the World War II, Vietnam, and Korean War Memorials, the National Museum of African American History, the White House Visitor Center, a number of Smithsonian museums, and George Washington’s home in Mount Vernon. “Although 14-year-olds are often famously hard to get a read on and they all like different things,” said Morgan, “the students were really intrigued by the Changing of the Guard at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier in Arlington Cemetery. The military ceremony was unlike anything they had seen.” She added that the eighth graders also enjoyed using a digital flight simulator and viewing the hangar and space shuttle at the Smithsonian Air and Space Museum, on their way back to the airport. “The kids all got a lot out of this unique experience flying across the country. For some, it was the first time they had traveled alone without their parents,” she said. The students stayed in a hotel in Maryland just outside Washington D.C. Two to four kids were assigned to respective suites, which each contained a kitchen, living room area, and sleeping areas. Along with the numerous sights, one highlight of the trip was a special tour of the Capitol arranged by Hunter and culminating in a meeting with Congressman Eric Swalwell of Dublin, with whom Hunter had worked in the DA’s office. Swalwell spoke with students for 20 minutes about his background and work in Congress, and his experience as a candidate for U.S. President. Morgan, who organized the trip, said, “It was the first year we’ve done something like this. I realized that many other middle schools have officially sanctioned D.C. trips, so I reached out to the PMS principal in late fall last year. When she said that the school couldn’t organize a trip like that due to ‘policy regulations,’ the other parents and I worked with an educational travel company, WorldStrides, to put it together.” Interested parents joined a Zoom call about the trip with a WorldStrides account representative last January. As students began signing up, Morgan, Hunter, and Smith began developing a detailed itinerary. “Given that there were only about 130 total students in the eighth grade class, it’s amazing that 40 enrolled in our first year holding this trip,” said Morgan. The trip remains a parent-run program. This year’s three chaperones are looking for next year’s organizers. “It was such a well-organized and positive experience. We’re looking for parents of rising eighth graders interested in taking it on for next year,” said Morgan. “It would be wonderful if this trip could continue to be a Piedmont Middle School tradition.” Interested parents are encouraged to contact Stacy Morgan at Stacy.Morgan94@gmail.com. articles.text: Recent discoveries unveil an astonishing 146 moons How many moons does Saturn have? In May, we would have said 83. Now, we’d say 146, nearly double what we had previously discovered. Dozens of small moons orbiting the planet Saturn were recently discovered by a team of astronomers led by Edward Ashton, using the Canadian-France-Hawaiian Telescope during a survey between 2019 and 2021. After analyzing data from the survey, the team identified about 80 previously unknown objects orbiting Saturn. These irregular moons are different from the bright object we see in the night sky and are shaped like potatoes. They may be leftovers of bigger moons that could have shattered in orbit. Moons can be fragmented by asteroids, comets and collisions between moons. Some moons orbit in retrograde, meaning the opposite way of other moons. It’s thought that they may orbit strangely because they were products of a more recent collision. The International Astronomical Union’s Minor Planet Center (MPC) is now reviewing the survey team’s data and confirming Photo courtesy of NASA/JPL/Space Science Institute their discoveries. Since May 3rd, the MPC formally recognized 60 new moons. This brings the total confirmed moon count for Saturn to more than 140. You may be aware of Saturn’s largest moon, Titan. The only moon in the solar system with a similar atmosphere nitrogen-rich atmosphere as Earth, Titan is home to clouds, lakes, seas, and rain of liquid hydrocarbons. There is a whole ocean underneath a thick layer of icy crust. There could be an entire world of life brewing beneath the surface, or the planet could be lifeless. These new discoveries mean Saturn has regained its title as the planet with the most moons. The planet Jupiter, with its stronger magnetic field, likely has more moons, but so far astronomers have only confirmed 92 moons around Jupiter. Saturn now has more moons than the rest of the planets combined. of coastal redwoods in the East Bay. articles.text: With only so many of our end-of-year awards to go around, some of the major contributions made throughout the year tend to get lost. In this article, we reflect on three athletes who were either entering their first year as a starter or getting time in a featured role for the first time in their PHS athletic career. Three who made a huge impact in the largest role of their time at Piedmont included Eva Levingston in basketball, threesport athlete Sam Shelby, and Albert Bellingrath in football and volleyball. Staff Photo Eva Levingston, PHS Class of 2023, was forced to miss her junior year due to transfer rules and became a main scorer, rebounder, and defender for the Highlanders as a senior. EVA LEVINGSTON Basketball Eva Levingston was perhaps the largest breakout performer at the school in 2022-23. After sitting out her junior year due to CIF transfer rules following her time at Alameda High, Levingston stepped into the Purple and White with a mission to prove that she was a major player. . She did just that, earning firstteam All-League honors in her only year at the school, continuously reeling in double-doubles for points and rebounds. She had 10 points and 14 rebounds in a 62-47 win over O’Dowd, 17 points and 10 rebounds in a 69-62 win over O’Dowd, and 21 points and over 10 rebounds in a 69-63 win over Salesian. Levingston will continue playing basketball at Cal State Fullerton. ALBERT BELLINGRATH Volleyball, Football SAM SHELBY Football, Soccer, Track Sam Shelby, a sophomore, is among the few three-sport athletes at the school. Even rarer is he’s a key player in each of the football, soccer and track teams. Shelby did it all on the football team, contributing as a receiver, running back, defensive back, return specialist, and he can pass—lining up at quarterback on occasion. He scored five Staff Photo Sam Shelby was a key three-sport athlete in football, soccer, and track as a sophomore. touchdowns on the varsity team before cancelation of its season. On the soccer team, Shelby appeared as a winger, using his speed to bomb down the flank. He earned starting minutes as a sophomore in Todd Sullivan’s system, contributing towards the team’s Division 4 North Coast Section title. With track in the recent spring season, Sam was a member of the squad’s 4x400 relay team which reached the CIF State Championship meet on May 26 alongside Christian Taylor, Parker Long, and Jack Zirkelbach-Ngai. Albert Bellingrath was a standout freshman on the volleyball team last spring and the JV football team back in the fall. On the volleyball team, Bellingrath earned starting time as a middle hitter, making a difference as a defensive and offensive threat. articles.text: CONCACAF Gold Cup starts Saturday International soccer is back for the United States Soccer Federation. The men’s team won the CONCACAF Nations League on Sunday, June 18 with a 2-0 victory over Canada, after bashing rival Mexico 3-0 in the semifinals on Thursday, June 15. Both games were played at Allegiant Stadium in Las Vegas. Their Nations League victory marked the United States’ fifth-consecutive victory of a major CONCACAF tournament. The U.S. won the Nations League in 2020, the Gold Cup in 2021, and now the Nations League in 2023. It was a heated semifinal game with Mexico. Midfielder Weston McKennie got a red card and had his jersey ripped. Sergino Dest nearly was red carded as well after getting in an altercation. He was subsequently pelted with beer cups. The baton for being the best team in CONCACAF seems to have passed from Mexico to the U.S.; the men’s team is undefeated through its six matches against El Tri at 4-2-0. The match with Mexico was marred by a brawl that resulted in the ejection of Mexico’s Cesar Miramontes and McKennie in the 69th and 71st minutes. Dest and Gerardo Arteaga’s skirmish in the 85th minute led to trash raining down on the players. Following the brawl, the match was halted twice due to Mexico fans chanting homophobic slurs. In the eighth minute of second-half stoppage time, referees called the match after the chant rang onto the broadcast. In the Finals versus Canada, the United States scored early in the 12th minute on a perfect cross from Gio Reyna, locating defender Chris Richard for a leaping header goal. Photo courtesy of CONCACAF Gold Cup The U.S. Men’s Soccer team now prepares for the 2023 Gold Cup with a very different roster than Nations League. The U.S. struck again in the 34th minute when newcomer Folarin Balogun scored on a right-footed rocket you love to see out of a striker. Balogun has dual citizenship with England and the U.S., and recently decided to play for the United States. He’s a product of Arsenal’s youth academy of the Premier League and came up through England’s youth system. Balogun has spent 2022-2023 on loan from Arsenal with Reims in France’s Ligue 1 and could become the answer the U.S. has been seeking at striker Gold Cup starts Saturday The United States Men’s National Team is set to take part in this year’s Gold Cup, stretching from June 24 through July 16. This year’s Gold Cup roster will look vastly different from what appeared in Nations League with a majority of players coming America’s major League. Soccer League. Instead of Christian Pulisic and Balogun leading the attack, the front line will likely include Earthquakes’ Cade Cowell and FC Dallas’ Jesús Ferreira. Goalkeeper Matt Turner is the only holdover player from the Nations League’s starting lineup. The Gold Cup features four groups of three teams with the top-two from each group advancing o the Quarterfinals. articles.text: The Tudors: Art and Majesty in Renaissance England opens Saturday The Legion of Honor, of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco, opens to the public this weekend an exhibit of historic significance. The Tudors: Art and Majesty in Renaissance England opens this Saturday, June 24. This is the first major exhibition in the United States of portraiture and decorative arts of the Tudor courts. It will include works from the museum’s collection, including a late 16th century panel painting, as well as tapestries commissioned or acquired by Henry VII and Henry VIII. “Few may be aware of the distinctive art and visual propaganda that was central to the splendor and drama of the Tudor court,” said Thomas Campbell, Director and CEO of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. “Now, in the first exhibition of its kind in the US, The Tudors: Art and Majesty in Renaissance England reunites scores of sumptuous paintings, precious jewels, rich tapestries and rare artifacts from collections around the world to bring the Tudor dynasty vividly to life–from the bloody founding of the dynasty in 1485 by Henry VII on the fields of Bosworth, to the final moments of Queen Elizabeth in 1603.” The Tudors: Art and Majesty in Renaissance England will be on view from June 24 through September 24. articles.text: Matthew McConaughey and Ryan Phillippe in The Lincoln Lawyer If you are a fan of writer Michael Connelly, then it’s possible you’ve read “The Lincoln Lawyer.” Connelly, once a Los Angeles crime reporter turned fiction writer, has created a memorable series of L.A.-based crime novels, many featuring detective Hieronymous Bosch. All are engaging reads. The Lincoln Lawyer is one of those bestselling novels, adapted to the screen by scriptwriter Joe Romano. Mickey Haller, the lead character, is a Los Angeles defense attorney, denizen of a chauffeured Lincoln Continental that he uses as his mobile office. He is the half-brother of Harry Bosch, and, like Harry, he’s flawed, street smart, resilient and guided by his own moral gyroscope. He can be a hard case when the need arises; but then working the gritty back streets of L.A. isn’t for the faint of heart. Matthew McConaughey, thankfully having moved beyond the sugarcoated, flash the six pack rom-coms of the last several years, chews up the L.A. scenery in this compelling whodunit. The corner-cutting Haller is his best role since A Time to Kill, a remarkable legal thriller based on John Grisham’s debut novel that was only picked up after he hit it big with The Firm. Haller takes his clients where he can find them, defending bikers and hookers, and, as is revealed, Louis Roulet (Ryan Phillippe), a rich kid from a prominent family, who is accused of raping and beating a prostitute who was working one of the downtown bars. While guilt or innocence is not relevant to providing a solid defense, and Mickey’s mantra is, ala Jerry McGuire, “show me the money,” he does acknowledge that the most terrifying client a lawyer can have is one who is innocent. And so Haller begins to peal the onion, building the defense, using his lead investigator, Frank Levin (William H. Macy). Levin’s no rookie, his face deeply lined, his eyes tired, his hair touching his shoulders. What’s the adage? It’s not your age, it’s the mileage. Like Mick, he’s intuitive, knows the streets, and is bulldog tenacious. Macy, one of the best character actors in films today, is exceptional, as are all of the actors in The Lincoln Lawyer, especially Marisa Tomei. articles.text: The Big Short is a muckraking blur of a movie. It’s filled with financial jargon – “credit-default swaps,” “collateralized debt,” “ninja loans,” “subprime mortgages,” “debt repackaging”. In the collective, it is arcane and delivered in dialogue that is manic and almost surreal. It also breaks the fourth-wall, that unspoken agreement between the audience and the characters in which they will not turn to the camera and speak directly to the moviegoer. It is a film of endless conversations, in boardrooms, offices, and hotel foyers that even those listening, the financial insiders, seem unable to fully grasp what they are being told. Having said that, The Big Short is one heck of a fine movie, riveting at times, because just enough of what is discussed makes sense While the film is intended to be a tragicomedy it is, ultimately, far more tragic than comedic. What is argued and explained and then bet on - big time – is that the housing bubble of 2007-2009 will pop like a carnival balloon and those who sell short will walk away with millions. articles.text: While The Stepfather is neither subtle nor shy, it does ratchet up serious tension as the film moves toward its predictable and harrowing conclusion. The story is familiar (it’s actually a remake of the 1987 movie of the same name) and aims at that primordial fear that we don’t really know the people we’re close to until it may be too late. David Harris (Dylan Walsh), charming and smooth, inserts himself into the lives of a mother, Susan Harding (Sela Ward), and her three children. Susan is just coming out of a divorce and is vulnerable. The kids are teens and adjusting to a split family and weekends with dad. Suddenly they have a supportive guy around, someone who often insists that all he values in life is family. He tells them, his wife and daughter were killed in a car accident more than a year ago. The screenwriters do an interesting thing at the outset. They make it clear to the audience that Harris is a psychopath and pure evil in the guise of a wonderful guy. In other words, the first shoe is immediately dropped. What gives the film an unrelenting tension is that the audience is waiting for the second shoe to drop. The test of the film is how effective the filmmakers are in revealing to the unsuspecting family that Harris is a stone-cold killer who is moving placidly among his victims with a wide smile and a loving, helpful persona. But all the while small chinks – ever so subtle, ever so easily explained – in his behavior begin to appear. It’s chilling to watch. Walsh, as an actor, does a superb job in transforming his face from barely controlled rage to wide smiles in mere seconds. Susan is oblivious. She’s in love. Her oldest son, Michael (Penn Bradley), however, begins to suspect that something is deeply wrong; however, his girlfriend (Amber Heard) insists that it is all in his imagination. The audience, of course, knows he’s right. The second shoe is about to fall. It’s only a matter of time. And it’s those minutes that make all the difference. As psych-horror films go, The Stepfather is well done. It’s a B-movie to be sure, one targeted at teens who unabashedly enjoy the genre and will surely turn out for this one. The Stepfather. At least not completely. There must also be magic and surprise. In other words, a film of this ilk will find more success if it’s a fable that asks young audiences to suspend their disbelief and climb on board – which, of course, they are fully prepared to do. Say, at the drop of a hat. But first, consider the book. Written by Maurice Sendak and published in 1963, it has sold 19 million copies worldwide, 10 million in the U.S. alone. Its success begs the question, Why? What is there about this story that young readers so completely embrace? The story, after all, comprises only 338 words; 41 lines of text; and is only 37 pages long. Perhaps it’s the fact that story is a seamless melding of reality and fantasy. Max, dressed in his wolf costume, consumed with a riptide of emotion, rebels, causing mischief, and is sent to his room. And that’s when the magic begins. His room grows into a forest and he finds a boat and sails to a distant shore where he discovers a band of feral monsters – large, furry, exotic, all strange hybrid animals. He becomes the king of the monsters, wears a crown, carries a scepter, and is empowered. It’s an overwhelming feeling for Max. He stands and yells to the monsters that it’s time to howl and experience their inner wildness. Eventually, however, he decides to return to his family, to those who love him most. Where the Wild Things Are is an elegant and simple story, wonderfully illustrated by Sendak, and one that would appeal to any youngster who feels conflicted and perhaps frustrated at being buffeted by the whims of family, school and siblings, who wishes only for a magic place where he or she can be king. In the first act of the film, Jonze captures, with pitch-perfect insight, the existential pain of any kid who feels overwhelmed by life. Max (Max Records) is coping with the divorce of his parents, and with a sense of isolation so complete that he talks to fences as if they could talk back. When Max discovers his mother has invited a strange man over for dinner, and sees then nuzzling on the couch, he acts out, argues with his mother and runs from the house, angry and conflicted. It’s at this point that Sendak’s fable begins. That is the real challenge for Jonze as a screenwriter. The difficulty of adapting Sendak’s story to the screen is that it lacks even a semblance of a strong narrative arc. There is only a paper-thin plot; there is no real conflict; there is no resolution. Hence, if Sendak’s book is going to be adapted to the screen as a 98-minute feature, Jonze will have to embellish considerably. But if he deviates too far from the fable template (and from Sendak’s book), he does so at his peril. Kids wish to be swept up in a story that involves, in some fashion, a journey akin to that found in Shrek or Harry Potter or Spy Kids, one in which the protagonist struggles to overcome adversity, achieves a specific goal, is victorious, and the tale ends with a nice moral. Jonze’s film draws very little from that recipe. Though the film is imaginative, and the photography superb, the tones are sepia and dark in contrast to the crisp, bright colors of most kids’ movies. It could be argued that Where the Wild Things Are is not a film intended for children, but for adults who enjoy watching movies that remind them of their childhood. The monsters, which Jonze develops, have names and speak; they don’t in the book. They are somber and dysfunctional, and Carol (James Gandolfini), the wild thing Max comes to know best, is given to bouts of scary temper, threatening to hurt Max. It’s even suggested that they should eat Max and they’re surprised that they haven’t. In the end, there is no emotional center to the film. Even the relationships between the wild things seem too subtle and strange, something that will be missed by the younger audience. It’s clear that Jonze made an astonishing effort to adapt a book that simply did not have enough substance to be made into feature film. It was a high-risk gamble by the studio and Jonze. But is it high gain? Where the Wild Things Are. Starring Catherine Keener, Max Records, James Gandolfini, Catherine O’Hara, Forest Whitaker and Chris Cooper. Directed by Spike Jonze. 1 hr., 41 min. The story is familiar (it’s actually a remake of the 1987 movie of the same name) and aims at that primordial fear that we don’t really know the people we’re close to until it may be too late. David Harris (Dylan Walsh), charming and smooth, inserts himself into the lives of a mother, Susan Harding (Sela Ward), and her three children. Susan is just coming out of a divorce and is vulnerable. The kids are teens and adjusting to a split family and weekends with dad. Suddenly they have a supportive guy around, someone who often insists that all he values in life is family. He tells them, his wife and daughter were killed in a car accident more than a year ago. The screenwriters do an interesting thing at the outset. They make it clear to the audience that Harris is a psychopath and pure evil in the guise of a wonderful guy. In other words, the first shoe is immediately dropped. What gives the film an unrelenting tension is that the audience is waiting for the second shoe to drop. The test of the film is how effective the filmmakers are in revealing to the unsuspecting family that Harris is a stone-cold killer who is moving placidly among his victims with a wide smile and a loving, helpful persona. But all the while small chinks – ever so subtle, ever so easily explained – in his behavior begin to appear. It’s chilling to watch. Walsh, as an actor, does a superb job in transforming his face from barely controlled rage to wide smiles in mere seconds. Susan is oblivious. She’s in love. Her oldest son, Michael (Penn Bradley), however, begins to suspect that something is deeply wrong; however, his girlfriend (Amber Heard) insists that it is all in his imagination. articles.text: Havens’ Avenue of Palms was for sale in 1922. They hired Houghton Sawyer, Albert Farr and Engineer Robert E. Carney to design a model city center. Continuing Farr’s Spanish Mission design at City Hall, their Master Plan called for an elaborate Exedra at the entrance to Piedmont Park, a grand threestory City Hall, additions to the current City Hall, a library, museum and municipal garages. They planned to re-route the streetcar line into a tunnel where passengers could enter and exit streetcars at an elegant plaza with a fountain at the park level. Passengers would not have to cross the streetcar tracks. The Master Plan was to be completed in phases, with each building to be approved by voters before construction. The grand three-story City Hall was scaled down to the present onestory Community Hall. Voters approved the first phase in 1924 which included funds to build the Exedra and the Community Hall. Later units of the Master Plan were never realized. School construction took precedence. The Junior High School and Wildwood School were built in 1923. Later bond issues failed to pass, and the Depression ended all thoughts of grand new construction. Piedmont’s new Community Hall and Exedra opened on April 3, 1925. Civic leaders and residents entered the newly landscaped Piedmont Park through the Exedra, which reporters compared to the “Arch of Triumph.” Guests admired Howard Gilkey’s new landscape design, with its rose garden behind the Exedra, extensive lawns and flowering shrubs along the path to the hall. The Community Hall was dedicated as a meeting place and social hall for all Piedmont residents. The lower level of the hall became the new armory for Piedmont’s Battery D of the 143rd Field Artillery. The land that became Guilford Road was sold as “Guilford Place” in 1921, and the land that became Palm Drive was sold as the Lower Piedmont Park Tract in 1922. In November of 1916, Piedmont voters defeated a measure to raise funds to purchase the parkland. Piedmont Park land was still available in 1921 when Piedmont philanthropist Wallace Alexander and others offered to purchase 14 acres of the park if the city would reimburse them. This plan allowed the entire 27-acre parcel to be sold. The School District could buy the 13 acres they wanted, and the city would have its park. Alexander purchased the land for the city in 1921 and one year later voters passed a bond issue, and the city reimbursed Wallace Alexander and his partners in full. Piedmont High School In 1921, construction began immediately on the high school. Architect William Weeks designed a reinforced concrete school with terra cotta trim for 500 students. The auditorium spanned the front of the school with two stories of classrooms behind. Two wings held more classrooms. The cooking and science labs were to be set away from the main building in these wings, removing any odors and fire risk. (The history of Piedmont High School will be explored in a later column.) New Municipal Park In 1922 the City Trustees went to work on a new civic center. The Oakland Tribune announced the sale of Piedmont Park in 1917. Development By 1916, Havens was planning to develop the park into residential home sites. He sent his art to San Francisco to be auctioned where paintings went to the new deYoung Museum, the Oakland Art Gallery (the predecessor of today’s Oakland Museum of California), and private collectors. (Havens’ art collection was described in my previous column published on December 5.) But Havens was in financial trouble. The Oakland Tribune Havens’ Avenue of Palms was for sale in 1922. They hired Houghton Sawyer, Albert Farr and Engineer Robert E. Carney to design a model city center. Continuing Farr’s Spanish Mission design at City Hall, their Master Plan called for an elaborate Exedra at the entrance to Piedmont Park, a grand threestory City Hall, additions to the current City Hall, a library, museum and municipal garages. They planned to re-route the streetcar line into a tunnel where passengers could enter and exit streetcars at an elegant plaza with a fountain at the park level. Passengers would not have to cross the streetcar tracks. The Master Plan was to be completed in phases, with each building to be approved by voters before construction. The grand three-story City Hall was scaled down to the present onestory Community Hall. Voters approved the first phase in 1924 which included funds to build the Exedra and the Community Hall. Later units of the Master Plan were never realized. School construction took precedence. The Junior High School and Wildwood School were built in 1923. Later bond issues failed to pass, and the Depression ended all thoughts of grand new construction. Piedmont’s new Community Hall and Exedra opened on April 3, 1925. Civic leaders and residents entered the newly landscaped Piedmont Park through the Exedra, which reporters compared to the “Arch of Triumph.” Guests admired Howard Gilkey’s new landscape design, with its rose garden behind the Exedra, extensive lawns and flowering shrubs along the path to the hall. The Community Hall was dedicated as a meeting place and social hall for all Piedmont residents. The lower level of the hall became the new armory for Piedmont’s Battery D of the 143rd Field Artillery. Piedmont Park had been saved The original Piedmont High School designed by William Weeks in 1921. from development. Only two small parts of the original park were sold to real estate developers. The land that became Guilford Road was sold as “Guilford Place” in 1921, and the land that became Palm Drive was sold as the Lower Piedmont Park Tract in 1922. Spanish-Inspired Chopped Salad with Shrimp Makes about 4 cups INGREDIENTS For the shrimp: • 4 large shrimp, 10-15 count • 1 large clove garlic, minced • 1 tablespoon Spanish olive oil, extra-virgin For the dressing: • 1 teaspoon Dijon mustard • 1 tablespoon sherry vinegar • 1-1/2 tablespoon Spanish olive oil, extra-virgin • 1 teaspoon fresh marjoram leaves, minced • 1/2 teaspoon Pimentón de La Vera dulce, aka smoked paprika • • 1/2 teaspoon black pepper, freshly ground 1/4 teaspoon sea salt, to taste For the salad: • 1 cup Persian cucumber, sliced into bite-sized chunks (substitute English cucumber) • 1 cup cherry tomatoes, halved • 1 cup firm, ripe avocado, about 1 medium, sliced into bite-sized chunks • 1/2 cup red bell pepper, about one-half of a medium pepper, diced • 1/2 cup red onion, about onehalf of a medium onion, diced • 1/4 cup f lat leaf parsley, coarsely chopped INSTRUCTIONS For the shrimp: If frozen, thaw in cold water, remove the shells and devein by slicing about 1/8-inch across the back of the shrimp and removing the “vein”. Heat the olive oil in a small frying pan over medium heat and add the garlic. When the garlic just barely begins to sizzle, add the shrimp. Cook until the first side becomes translucent, only takes 2-3 minutes. Turn the shrimp and move them about the pan to keep the garlic moving too. It was noted that the columns are missing lanterns on their tops. Mike Henn told the story from his days on the City Planning Commission that the neighborhood once wanted the City to put replicas of the originals on the columns. However, neither the residents nor the City wanted to pay for them, so it never happened. There is still electricity in the columns if anyone wants to install them. The walkers also noted the distinctive four brown tiles that are inlayed in each section of the concrete sidewalks that were part of the original St. James residential development. At the end of St. James at Park Blvd., some walkers needed to head back, but one block down Park, just past Trestle Glen Road, is Cavendish Lane. Some walkers wanted to see it. This is a narrow street that looks like an alley. It is in Oakland, but there are four homes with Piedmont addresses at its end. The street was damaged in February 2017 after it was undermined by heavy rains and a faulty construction project on a Trestle Glen home below. The hillside and road slipped away, and the Piedmont families were unable to access their homes by car for six weeks. The City of Piedmont made temporary fixes, but permanent repairs by Oakland were not begun until two years later. After walking a few hundred feet the group saw the previously damaged roadway with a very large blue tarp covering the hillside below a retaining wall. A Piedmont Public Works notice, dated August 2021, was a taped on it and said all construction work was to be stopped because of violations of City ordinances. By Cookie Segelstein Dear MacMama: My husband who is a Windows user always complains that my computer is running software that is too old. My Mac is a 2019 iMac, and I am still running the software that came on it, which is I think Mojave. Is it really a bad idea not to keep it up to date? And can my Mac even run the latest? –Leena P., Oakland Dear Leena: Although I never like to get in the middle of a computer marriage squabble, in this case I must side with your hubby. Of course, I understand that it takes quite a while to get used to a new machine as well as a new operating system (OS) like Mojave and software. And in some cases, especially when there are big changes, waiting a bit to upgrade for a few months won’t hurt. But Mojave is 4 operating systems (and this doesn’t even count the supplemental updates) behind the current one, which is Ventura. And a new one is coming out in October. And your machine can definitely run the current OS, assuming you have enough space on your hard drive. There have been some big changes in the user experience with the newer operating systems. Basically, one of the main changes, is that each of the operating systems make all of your devices work together better. Here are some reasons to keep your computer’s OS up to date. By the way, the OS is the software that manages your experience on the computer, including supporting applications like Safari, Mail, Pages, etc. 1. The longer you wait, the more extreme the changes will be. So, for example if you wait for 3-4 years to upgrade, the way Mac Mail and Safari works will take longer to get used to. Also, for example System Preferences has been changed to System Settings. It’s a very different interface and takes a bit to get used to. When you upgrade regularly, the changes seem more gradual. 2. Many of the updates are bug fixes. So, if an application has been found to be unstable, often the update fixes it. 3. Drivers for your printers, scanners and other devices may become out of date. And some of the newer printers will need new updated drivers, which the newer OS versions will have, but the older ones may not. 4. The older your Mac’s OS is, the less secure it is. Even though Macs generally are less vulnerable to viruses and hackers, malware is designed to exploit loopholes in an operating system’s security design infrastructure. Apple often releases software patches to ensure your Mac is as secure as possible. In some cases, some websites will not open with older browsers (Safari, Chrome and Firefox are browsers), as they are not considered secure. And browsers like Safari get updates often, as hackers and malware get more invasive. 5. New OS versions always come with new features. One of the best features in the current OS (Ventura) is Continuity Camera, which allows you to use your iPhone as a webcam. I found this to be a game changer for me, as the iPhone 14 has a fantastic camera. 6. New versions of some software won’t work on older operating systems, or at least are not supported. For example, most of the games on the App store will not work on anything before OS Monterey, which is 3 versions newer than yours. Of course, there are some reasons not to upgrade. If you depend on software that is no longer being updated (like early versions of Photoshop, ProTools, iWeb, MuseScore and even early versions Microsoft Office), you may want to stick to your older OS to be able to continue using those applications. And the newer operating systems break the compatibility with some of the older software. I know several people who keep an older machine around for that very reason. And if you want to make sure that your Mac download updates automatically, here’s how you do it on Mojave (also Monterey, Big Sur and Catalina). Open System Preferences, click on Software Update, check the box beside Automatically keep my Mac up to date (or Download new updates when available). Then select the box Install macOS updates. It is prudent to keep things as up to date as possible, if for no other reason than safety and security. The last owner, Sam Mazza, was an eccentric gentleman who purchased the castle in 1929 for $29,000, as a place to store the thousands of antiques he had collected over the years. articles.text: Dear Jim: We are about to start a remodel and are debating about whether to hire a designer and then a contractor, or whether we should do design-build with a single firm. Your thoughts? –Austin H. Know yourself A decision about how you want the design aspects of your project to occur should be made and stuck to. Will you be hands-on, making the bulk of the selections and design decisions? Or will you want the contractor or designer to make choices and provide you with selections to choose from? This may seem simple, but in our experience the matter of how you want to work is decided early on to avoid mistakes. Know your designer Finding and sourcing compatible fixtures, cabinets, tile, flooring, paint colors, etc. are all skills that most designers possess. However, some lack the construction knowledge needed to integrate their choices into architectural drawings and construction work. In a recent project, our client’s designer didn’t read our architect’s drawing properly and ordered a vanity that was too wide, had to be returned, and reordered, causing project delays Recessing appliances and closets into the crawlspace of this basement second unit created much needed working space. and high return shipping and restocking fees. Get to know your project First, decide on your level of involvement. Often clients tell us they are hands-off, then change their minds and want to be more involved later in the game. Understand that any changes in the design-build process, including increasing your involvement can significantly affect timelines, budget and choices. Next, make sure your contractor or design-builder has clear expectations on the decision-making process for items being selected and ordered, and the time frames for delivery and budget. Keep in mind that the current supply chains are erratic. Having to return and reorder supplies may sideline a project. Finally, in addition to your designer and contractor being a good fit for you, be sure your selections properly fit the space and are reviewed by the contractor, designer and you before being ordered. Measure twice and cut once applies to the design process, too. The current turf is well beyond its eight-year life span. In 2007, when it was installed, the new turf cost $219,000; installation took two weeks.
